newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU warns against privatisations restrictions. [Corrected 18:43 gmt]
newsitem.headline: EU warns against privatisations restrictions. [Corrected 18:43 gmt]

text.p: The European Commission warned national governments on Wednesday they must not discriminate against investors from other EU countries (corrects from "foreign investors") in privatisation programmes.
At issue are measures often designed to prevent companies slated for privatisation from falling into foreign hands.

In a communication aimed at clarifying the application of EU rules on the free movement of capital to investment within the 15-nation bloc, the Commission said discriminatory measures based on nationality would only be tolerated if justified on public security and defence grounds.
"Restrictions which apply exclusively to investors who are nationals of other Union member states will be judged to be incompatible with the (EU) treaty," it said in a statement.

The Commission appears to be particularly concerned with 1994 Italian legislation which requires prior government approval for the acquisition of important stakes in utilities previously controlled by the state.
Commission officials particularly singled out the on-going privatisation of Italian energy group ENI which started in November 1995.

Italy is expected to sell soon a third tranche of shares in ENI, but Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi has said the state's holding will not fall below 51 percent. The Treasury currently holds 69 percent.
But the Commission was also worried about discriminatory measures in other countries, the sources said, adding that they were constantly receiving complaints from disgruntled investors.

They cited British legislation adopted in 1975 as potentially harmful although they noted it had not been used for a long time. They also mentionned problems with the privatisation of French oil group Elf Aquitaine.

The Commission has forced the Portuguese government to change a 1990 privatisation law which set limits on the amount of shares a foreign investor could buy and also put restrictions on the reselling shares bought in an initial offering. This was the only time it has openly intervened to put an end to discriminatory measurs.
